2027-06-19.title: Saturday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time · St Romuald
readings: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness
Taste and see the goodness of the Lord
Strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well
2027-06-19.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). St Romuald, abbot, may be remembered (optional memorial); by the traditional reckoning he died on 19 June 1027, so this year marks a thousand years since his death. A Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may also be celebrated. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Psalm 34:8–13 = NRSV 34:7–12). Liturgical colour: green (white if a memorial is kept).
2027-06-19.verse: but he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” So, I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.
theo: For several days Paul has been answering people in Corinth who compared him with smooth, impressive preachers and found him wanting. Today he reaches the strangest part of his defence. If they want boasting, he will boast, but of what? First he speaks, almost shyly, in the third person: “I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven.” He was “caught up into Paradise and heard things that are not to be told, that no mortal is permitted to repeat.” Then he refuses to build anything on it: “On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses.” The revelation is real, but he will not let the Corinthians judge him by it. And now the heart of the passage: “to keep me from being too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me.” We do not know what the thorn was. Some of the Fathers thought of a sickness, others of persecution or of a temptation; Paul never tells us, and perhaps that is a mercy, because every reader can place his own thorn beside Paul's. “Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me.” Paul prayed, and prayed again, as Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane. The answer was not the one he asked for: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” The thorn stayed; the grace came. And Paul's whole way of seeing changed: “Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.” The Psalm is the song of a poor man who learned the same thing: “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. O taste and see that the LORD is good; happy are those who take refuge in him.”

The Gospel continues the Sermon on the Mount, and Jesus speaks to people who knew what it was to worry about tomorrow's food. He begins with a choice: “No one can serve two masters … You cannot serve God and wealth.” Then he goes to the root of so much of our anxiety: “do not worry about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, or about your body, what you will wear.” He does not tell us to stop working. He tells us to look: “Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.” Worry adds nothing: “can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?” The answer is not carelessness but a new order of things: “But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” And then a word of great kindness: “So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will bring worries of its own. Today's trouble is enough for today.” Paul and Jesus say the same thing from two sides: God's grace is enough for today's weakness, and today's bread is enough for today. St Romuald, remembered today, was a young nobleman of Ravenna who turned from a violent world to a life of prayer, and spent his long life founding hermitages and monasteries in Italy; the best known is Camaldoli, in the hills near Arezzo. His followers kept a short rule attributed to him which begins, in substance: sit in your cell as in paradise, and watch your thoughts as a good fisherman watches for fish. It is the Gospel of the lilies put into practice: a heart at rest in God, seeking first his kingdom.
outline: Ask: what is the one worry that woke you up most often this month?
Paul prays three times and receives not removal but grace.
Point 2 · Power made perfect in weakness
Our weakness becomes the place where Christ's power lives.
Point 3 · Look at the birds, consider the lilies
Seek first the kingdom, and live one day at a time.
live: Bring to the Lord in prayer today one weakness you have asked him many times to remove, and ask instead for the grace to carry it.
Write down tonight the worries you have for tomorrow, place the paper under your Bible or a crucifix, and leave them there till morning.
saints: Born in Ravenna of a noble family, he turned to God as a young man after his father killed a relative in a quarrel, and did penance as a monk at Sant'Apollinare in Classe. Drawn to solitude, he lived for a time under a hermit's guidance and then spent decades travelling through Italy, reforming monasteries and founding hermitages. The best known is Camaldoli, near Arezzo, from which came the Camaldolese Benedictines, who unite the common life of monks with the solitary life of hermits. He died, by the traditional account, on 19 June 1027 at Val di Castro.
2027-06-19.prayer: Lord God, you know the thorn each of us carries and the worries that keep us awake. When we ask you to take them away and you do not, give us the grace that is sufficient, and let the power of Christ dwell in our weakness. Teach us to look at the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, to seek first your kingdom and its righteousness, and to leave tomorrow in your hands. Through the prayers of St Romuald, give us hearts at rest in you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Before Communion the priest shows us the Host and we answer: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. We come to the altar not because we are strong but because we are weak, and the Bread of Life is the grace that is sufficient for this day. Each Mass is our daily bread, given one day at a time.

quick: Paul boasts not of his visions but of his weakness: a thorn in the flesh that the Lord did not remove.
The Lord answered Paul's prayer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”
Jesus tells us not to worry: look at the birds and the lilies, seek first God's kingdom, and let today's trouble be enough for today.
2027-06-19.action: Hand over one worry to God today in a short prayer each time it comes back to your mind.
2027-06-19.question: What do I serve first: God, or the security that money seems to promise?
kidsaint: Romuald was a rich young man in Italy about a thousand years ago. He was sad when he saw how much people fought and hurt each other, so he decided to give his life to God. He went to live as a monk, and later as a hermit, praying alone in a small hut in the hills. Many people came to learn from him, and he started many little houses of prayer, the most famous one at a place called Camaldoli. He taught his monks to sit quietly with God, as if they were already in paradise. Lesson: find a quiet minute every day to sit with God and tell him your worries.

family.explain: Jesus pointed to the birds and said: they do not plant rice or keep it in a store, but God feeds them. He pointed to the wild flowers and said: they do not sew clothes, but God dresses them more beautifully than a king. If God takes care of birds and flowers, he will surely take care of us. So we work hard, but we do not need to be afraid.
family.intention: We pray for families who are worried about school fees, rent or food this month, and for those who have lost work in the monsoon rains.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one worry in our family that we can give to God together tonight?”

illus: A young mother in Thrissur had saved for months for her children's school bags and uniforms, and then the monsoon flooded the ground floor of her house the week before school reopened. She sat on the stairs, she said later, counting what was lost. Her small son brought her a bird's feather he had found on the wet veranda and asked why birds do not get cold in the rain. She laughed for the first time that day, and remembered the Gospel of the birds of the air. Neighbours from the parish came the next morning with buckets and two old school bags. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you know our weakness and our worries. Let your grace be enough for us today, and teach us to seek first your kingdom. Amen.
share: A thorn was given me in the flesh (2 Corinthians 12:7). Is there a weakness in my life that God may be using to keep me humble and close to him?
My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). When have I experienced God's strength at a moment when I felt weakest?
Do not worry about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34). Which worry about tomorrow is stealing my peace today?
pm.resp: Taste and see the goodness of the Lord.
interc: For the sick and those who carry long illnesses, that they may find Christ's power in their weakness.
For parents anxious about the new school year, and for children beginning new classes, that they may trust the Father who feeds the birds.
For all who are tempted to serve money above God, that they may seek first his kingdom.
For monks, nuns and hermits, especially the Camaldolese, on the thousandth anniversary of St Romuald's death, that their prayer may sustain the Church.
For our group, that we may live one day at a time in the care of our heavenly Father.
pm.close: Father, you clothe the lilies and feed the birds of the air. Keep us in your care, and let the power of Christ dwell in us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul was a great apostle. He had seen visions, he had been caught up into Paradise, as he tells us today. But when the Corinthians asked him for proof that he was a true apostle, he did not show them his visions. He showed them his weakness. On my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses (2 Corinthians 12:5).

He speaks of a thorn in the flesh. We do not know what it was: an illness, a persecution, a temptation. Paul prayed three times that it would leave him. And the Lord answered: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn did not go. But grace came. Sometimes God answers our prayer not by taking away the burden but by giving us the strength to carry it.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks to people who worried, just as we do, about food and clothes and the future. Look at the birds of the air, he says; consider the lilies of the field (Matthew 6:26, 28). He does not say: do not work. He says: do not let worry be your master. You cannot serve God and wealth. Worry cannot add a single hour to our life. It can only steal the peace of today.

So Jesus gives us an order of life: strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well (Matthew 6:33). And he gives us a measure: today's trouble is enough for today. St Romuald, whom we remember today, taught his monks to sit with God as if they were already in paradise. Let us also find a quiet minute today, give God our thorn and our worries, and receive the grace that is enough. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever watched the crows and sparrows outside your window? They do not go to the market and they do not cook food, but God feeds them every day. Jesus said: if God takes care of the birds, he will take care of you too, because you are much more precious to him! So when you feel worried about an exam or a new class, say: Jesus, I trust you. Then do your best, and let him take care of the rest.

intro: Theme: “My grace is sufficient for you.”
A thorn that stayed, a grace that came, and a Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.

sub: Visions Paul will not boast of.
q: He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me,
points.apply: Pray today for the grace to carry the burden God has not yet taken away, instead of only asking him to remove it.

sub: Weakness as a dwelling for Christ.

concl: Paul learned that grace is sufficient and that Christ's power lives in our weakness.
Jesus teaches us to seek first the kingdom and to leave tomorrow in the Father's hands.
2027-06-19.resolve: Give one worry to God each day this week, and do today's work in peace.
